sections.introduction: Vip3 is an insecticidal toxin isolated from Bacillus thuringiensis (Estruch et al. 1996;Yu et al. 1997;Van Rie 2000;Bhalla et al. 2005;Crickmore et al. 2006;Fang et al. 2007). However, its amino acid sequence shares no similarity with any known Bt d -endotoxins, which have been extensively studied and widely utilized for transgenic insect control (Mehlo et al. 2005). Vip3 is produced and secreted during the vegetative growth stage while d -endotoxins are expressed during the sporulation stage (Estruch et al. 1996;Yu et al. 1997;Donovan et al. 2001). Vip3 and its homologous genes have been identified from different Bt strains (Shen et al. 2003;Miles et al. 2004;Bhalla et al. 2005;Rang et al. 2005;Crickmore et al. 2006), and most of them are highly active against broad species within Lepidoptera (Estruch et al. 1996;Mesrati et al. 2005). Vip3 was believed to be activated by trypsin digestion through generation of a 62-kDa polypeptide core, similar to the activation of the d -endotoxins (Lee et al. 2003). Vip3 appears to bind to insect midgut epithelium specific membrane proteins of 80-and 100-kDa, which are different from those bonded by crystal toxins (Lee et al. 2003(Lee et al. , 2006)). Thus, Vip3 is likely to have a different mode of action from the crystal toxins and could be a valuable alternative candidate gene for the new generation of transgenic crops for insect resistance management. However, so far very few studies were reported on Vip3 protein biochemistry and on activity improvement by creating mutants. In this report, we present our studies on characterization of five mutants of Vip3AcAa on their insecticidal activities and sensitivity to trypsin digestion. Vip3AcAa is a hybrid gene of vip3Ac1 and vip3Aa1 obtained in our previous study by combining DNA fragments encoding the N-terminal part of the 600 amino acid residues of Vip3Ac1 and C-terminal part of the 190 amino acid residues of Vip3Aa1 (Fang et al. 2007). ## Generation of vip3 mutant genes All DNA manipulations including PCR, restriction digestion, ligation, agrose gel electrophoresis and transformation, were carried out as described by Sambrook et al. (1989). The 2.37-kb full-length vip3AcAa gene was amplified from the plasmid supplied by Fang et al. (2007) with a pair of primers which were anchored with a Bgl II and a Xho I restriction site, respectively (V3Bgl II 5'GGCTAGATCTatg AACAAGAATAATAC-TAAATTAAGC and V3XhoI 5'AGAGCTCGAGttaCT TAATAGAGACATCG-TAAAAATC, with the restriction sites being underlined, and the initiation codon and stop codon were in lower case). The PCR product was purified and cloned into pMD18-T (TaKaRa). A clone confirmed by sequencing was used as the template in PCR for generating the mutants. Except the 62-kDa N-terminal deletion mutant, all the other vip3 mutants were created by PCR using the common forward primer described above, V3Bgl II, and a mutation-inducing reverse primer. The reverse primer for vip3add is v3add (5'AGAGCTCGAGCCCCTTAATAGAGACATCGTAAAAATC), in which the original stop codon was removed. The reverse primer for vip3del is v3del (5'AGAGCTCGAGttaGACATCGTAAAAATGTACAATAGGAC), in which the nine nucleotides (CTTAATAGA) encoding the last three amino acid residues were deleted. A degenerate reverse primer c3xxx (5'AGAGCTCGAGttaTYBAANAGA-GACATCGTAAAAATGTACAAT, Y 0T/C, B0T/C/G, N 0A/T/C/G) was used to amplify a pool of mutants with mutations at the last two residues. Based on biological activity screening, two mutants, one with highest activity, vip3m11 , and the other with no activity, vip3m9 , were selected for this study. V3-62k (5'GGCTAGATCTatgGA-TAGCTCGCCTGCTGATATTCTTG) and V3Xho I were used to amplify the nucleotide sequence encoding the 62-kDa N-terminal deletion mutant Vip3-62k. The forward primer V3-62k was designed according to the first protoxin processing site of Vip3A in the lepidopteron gut (Estruch et al. 1996). All the PCR amplifications were carried out with high fidelity pyrobest DNA Polymerase (TaKaRa). After 'A' tailing reaction with Taq DNA polymerase, the PCR products were cloned into pMD18-T. The accuracy of the genes was verified by sequencing. The confirmed DNA fragments of the vip3 mutants genes in pMD18-T were digested out with Bgl II and Xho I, and then cloned into pET-28a (Novagen) predigested with Bam HI and XhoI (Bgl II and Bam HI are cohesive ends) for expression. ## Expression of vip3 mutants in E. coli The pET-28a based expression plasmids were transformed into competent cells of BL21-Star (DE3). A single colony was picked for starting culture with Luria ÁBertani medium (LB) containing kanamycin (100 mg/mL) in a shaking incubator at 250 rpm at 378C. When the optical density of the cell culture reached 0.6 at 600nm, the cells were induced for expression by Isopropylthio-d-galactoside (IPTG) at 1 mM final concentration. After 6 h of induction at 308C and 250 rpm, the cells were harvested by centrifugation for 10 min at 3000 )g , and then resuspended and sonicated in PBS buffer (137 mM NaCl, 2.7 mM KCl, 10 mM Na 2 HPO 4 , 2 mM KH 2 PO 4 ) for bioassay and for trypsin resistance testing. The total sonicated cell lysate of each sample was examined by sodium dodecyl sulfate Ápolyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS ÁPAGE) analysis, and the Vip3 proteins in the samples were densitometrically quantified in gel using the VersaDoc imaging system and the image analysis software Quantity One from Bio-Rad Laboratories (Hercules, CA). A series of concentrations of bovine serum albumin (0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 0.8, 1.0, and 2.0 mg per lane) was used as the standard. ## Trypsin assay and Western blotting analysis The total sonicated cell lysate of each sample was treated for 1 h at 378C by gradient concentrations of trypsin of 0, 0.005, 0.01, 0.025, 0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0, 2.5, 5.0, and 10 mg/mL. The digested samples were analyzed by 10% SDS ÁPAGE. For Western blotting analysis, proteins treated by 1.0 mg/mL trypsin at 378C for 1 h were separated by SDS ÁPAGE and transferred onto nitrocellulose membranes. Vip3-specific antiserum from rabbit was used as the primary antibody, and the goat anti-rabbit IgG conjugated with HRP was used as the secondary antibody. The blotting signals were visualized with diaminobenzidine (DAB-4HCl) and 0.1% H 2 O 2 . ## Insecticidal activity bioassay Bioassays were conducted with cotton bollworm, Helicoverpa armigera , and beet armyworm, Spodoptera exigua , in Multiwell-24 plates feeding on the artificial diet (Mu et al. 2002). Each assay sample was diluted into six different concentrations, and then each was evenly spread on the surface of the diet. After drying by evaporation on a rocking shaker, neonates were set into the assay wells for bioassay at 308C. A single neonate was placed into each well for cotton bollworm while four neonates were placed in each well for beet armyworm. PBS buffer and E. coli strain BL21 with empty pET-28a were used as the negative controls. A total of 24 neonates were used for assay of each sample, and each assay was repeated for three times. The assay results were read 7 days after the start of the assays. LC 50 is defined as the concentration of toxin Bacillus thuringiensis Vip3 mutant proteins 701 that caused 50% mortality of the neonates, and was calculated based on probity analysis using the statistical software POLO as described by Kain et al. (2004). ## Selection of the vip3 mutants of the last two C-terminal residues In our previous study, we noticed accidentally that the last few residues are critical to the activity of Vip3s. By PCR using a degenerated primer, we obtained a total of 15 different mutants. The insecticidal activities of the E. coli expressed proteins of these mutants were assayed against cotton bollworm and beet armyworm at a high concentration. Only one mutant, Vip3m11, was found to be highly toxic to both of the lepidopteran insects tested. The last two residues of Vip3m11 mutated from IK to LR. Thus, Vip3m11 was selected for further characterization. Most of the other mutants either totally lost activity or only maintained activity of delaying growth of the beet armyworms. An inactive mutant Vip3m9, which possessed a terminal lysine to glycine mutation, was selected as a negative control. ## Cloning and expression of vip3 mutants in E. coli The full-length gene of vip3AcAa , as well as its four mutants with alternations at the very C-terminal sequence (Table I) were generated and expressed in E. coli (Figure 1). Vip3del is a mutant with the deletion of the last three amino acid residues, and Vip3add with an addition of eight residues (Leu ÁGlu ÁHis ÁHis ÁHis ÁHis ÁHis ÁHis) at its C-terminus. Vip3m11 and Vip3m9 were two mutants of the last two residues of the C-terminus as described above. The Vip3-62k mutant protein resulted from the deletion of N-terminal 198 amino acid residues of the full-length protein of Vip3AcAa, which has 789 amino acid residues and a molecular weight of about 88 kDa. SDS ÁPAGE analysis suggested that they were all over-expressed in E. coli with approximately the expected sizes based on the estimation of mobility (Figure 1). ## Biological activity The insecticidal activity of the Vip3 mutant proteins were assayed using two common lepidopteran insects, cotton bollworm and beet armyworm. Vip3del and Vip3add did not cause any mortality or growth inhibition to both insects even at very high dose (20 mg/cm 2 ), suggesting that the minimal C-terminal deletion and addition resulted in the total loss of activity in our study. However, the activity of the substitution mutants of the last two amino acid residues varies from total loss of activity to gain of activity against beet armyworm. The LC 50 of Vip3m11 is 4.27 ng/cm 2 for beet armyworm, Table I. The C-terminal amino acid sequence of Vip3 mutants. Vip3 mutants C-terminal amino acid sequence Vip3AaAc . . . YGGPIVHFYDVSIK Vip3del . . . YGGPIVHFYDV Vip3add . . . YGGPIVHFYDVSIKLEHHHHHH Vip3m11 . . . YGGPIVHFYDVSLR Vip3m9 . . . YGGPIVHFYDVSLG compared to 73.0 ng/cm 2 for the original protein (Table II). The activity difference against cotton bollworm is not as significant (Table II). It appears that the mutation of the last residue to a conservative residue (K to R) would enhance the activity, while the mutation to a non-conservative residue (K to G) could abolish activity. ## Stability under trypsin digestion To better understand the observation of the loss of activity of the Vip3 mutants generated in this study, their stability against trypsin digestion was studied. Vip3Aa1 generates a trypsin resistant 62-kDa polypeptide when digested with trypsin (Yu et al. 1997;Lee et al. 2003Lee et al. , 2006)). This study also showed that the original toxin Vip3AcAa generated a 62-kDa polypeptide that is resistant to very high concentration of trypsin (Figure 2A). So did the active mutant Vip3m11 (Figure 2B). However, the inactive mutants were all found to be senstive to typsin digestion (Figure 2C ÁE). Although a weak 62-kDa polypeptide signal appeared in the digested products of Vip3m9 at low levels of trypsin, it disappeared at the increased concentrations of trypsin (Figure 2C). Western analysis using the Vip3 antiserum confirmed the observation (Figure 3). This study clearly demonstrated that the inactive mutants were senstive to trypsin digestion and the stable 62-kDa core could be a hallmark of active insecticidal Vip3 proteins. Table II. sections.discussion: This study suggests that the Vip3 C-terminus is critical to its insecticidal activity and might be the region for protein engineering for activity improvement. The observation that the changes of the two very C-terminal amino acid residues (IK to LR) of Vip3 led to the significant improvement of its insecticidal activity against beet armyworm demonstrated the possibility of activity improvement by generating and screening C-terminal mutants. Protein engineering has been successfully used to generate improved Bt d-endotoxins with higher and broader insecticidal activity (Rajamohan et al. 1996;Chen et al. 2006). The same might be done in Vip3. Numerous Vip3 homologous proteins have been isolated recently (Doss et al. 2002;Bhalla et al. 2005;Rang et al. 2005;Crickmore et al. 2006;Fang et al. 2007). The alignment of these Vip3s reveals that the N-terminal part of about 600 amino acid 116 66 35 45 kDa M Figure 4. SDS ÁPAGE analysis of the trypsin digestion products of Vip3-62k polypeptide. The black triangle indicates the gradient concentration of trypsin in the reaction, including final concentration of 0, 0.005, 0.01, 0.025, 0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0, 2.5, 5.0, and 10 mg/mL (from left to right). Bacillus thuringiensis Vip3 mutant proteins 705 residues is highly conserved, while the C-terminal part of about 190 amino acid residues is much less conserved. One might infer that the C-terminus might be more tolerant to the mutations. However, our study suggested the opposite; the C-terminal part is critical for maintaining the activity, as demonstrated by the loss of activity by the addition or deletion of a few amino acid residues at the C-terminus. Thus, the C-terminal variations among the different Vip3 proteins may have resulted from the selection for diversified activities rather than the accumulation of random mutations during the evolution of the vip3 family. Resistance to trypsin and other proteases is a major biochemical characteristic of insecticidal proteins targeting the midgut. Without resistance to proteases, toxins will be readily destroyed in insect guts by various gut proteases. Forcada et al. (1996) found that midgut proteases from a Bt-resistant strain of H. virescens processes protoxin slower but it degrades the active toxin faster than the susceptible strain. The increased degradation rate of the Bt toxin may also account for its loss of sensitivity to fifth instar larvae (Keller et al. 1996). The rightly folded Vip3 may form a tightly structured protease resistant core, while the deletion, addition and some mutations at the C-terminus may have resulted to the disruption of the three dimensional structures of the Vip3s, which rendered them sensitive for attacks by proteases. Thus, the 62-kDa trypsin resistant core could be a hallmark of active insecticidal Vip3 proteins. Surprisingly, the 62-kDa polypeptide expressed from E. coli is not active. The fact that this inactive 62-kDa fragment is highly sensitive to trypsin suggests that the polypeptide is not folded correctly into a functional insecticidal protein. Thus, the N-terminal part may serve as a folding driver for the Vip3 proteins and is likely required for the correct folding of the Vip3 protein. However, this N-terminal part is later removed and not required for the final stages of the toxic process. Rather, the N-terminal part may need to be removed to activate the protein (Lee et al. 2003). The N-terminal 31 residues of the Vip3 protein was believed to be the secretion signal peptide (Estruch et al. 1996), but it is not a typical one as it is not removed in the secreted mature protein. Furthermore, part of the secretion signal is essential for the insecticidal activity (data not shown). Although we did not test a wide spectrum of lepidopteron insects for the activity of the Vip3 mutants we generated in this study, it is likely that the inactive ones are not active against other species, as indicated by their high sensitivity to trypsin in this study. However, Selvapandiyan et al. (2001) found that a Vip3 with a large C-terminal fragment (154 amino acid residues) deletion remained active to Chilo partellus (spotted stalk borer). It is unknown if that deletion mutant was sensitive or resistant to trypsin. Because we did not have access to C. partellus , we do not know if our mutants are actually also active against this insect.
